Nigeria and Togo have signed a memorandum of understanding to develop two interconnected data parks, seeking private investment to attract global data centre operators and strengthen digital infrastructure across West Africa. The agreement was signed in Lagos on Thursday by Nigeria’s Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr Bosun Tijani, and Togo’s Minister of Digital Economy and Transformation, Cina Lawson. The project is expected to commence in the second quarter of 2027, subject to the successful completion of the necessary preparations. A data park is a designated area equipped with shared infrastructure, including reliable electricity, fibre-optic connectivity, serviced land and cooling facilities, where multiple companies can establish data centres. Unlike individual data centres, which house servers used to store and process digital information, a data park provides the supporting infrastructure for several operators. Under the proposed arrangement, the two countries will develop separate but interconnected facilities through a joint special purpose vehicle in which both governments will hold equity alongside private companies and investors. Speaking during the signing, Tijani said the structure was designed to attract private capital rather than leave the governments responsible for financing the entire development. “The way this has been structured is that it’s going to be a special purpose vehicle where the government will have equity in the vehicle, a single vehicle. Both the Nigerian government and Togo’s government will have equity in it. But we will also have private companies and investors who would join us in that vehicle,” he said. He added that the governments would focus on regulatory support and creating an attractive investment environment to encourage international operators to establish facilities in the parks. I think the biggest contribution for the government is on the regulation side, because we want the park to be as attractive as possible,” he stated. Lawson described the agreement as the first joint digital infrastructure project between Nigeria and Togo, saying it reflected a broader ambition to develop large-scale projects through regional cooperation. The Togolese minister said the partnership would help attract operators and customers from both French-speaking and English-speaking markets across West Africa. “This collaboration is also significant because Togo is a French-speaking country, Nigeria is an English-speaking country, and so what we want to do is that we want to be able to attract both French-speaking and English-speaking countries,” Lawson said. Lawson also linked the initiative to Togo’s fibre-optic expansion programme, which she said was targeting connections to 2,700 schools, 250 hospitals and all districts in the country. She disclosed that both countries had also discussed developing artificial intelligence data centres in the future, arguing that Africa should participate in the expansion of global AI computing infrastructure. Nigeria is considering a site adjoining Egbin Power Station in Lagos State, while Togo is assessing candidate locations for its facility. Tijani said both parks were expected to become operational around the same time, although Togo had yet to select its final location. He said Egbin was attractive because of its proximity to power generation infrastructure, access to gas and water resources for cooling, and potential connectivity through fibre-optic and submarine cable networks. Tijani said the ambition was to attract operators capable of serving international markets rather than limit the facilities to regional demand. “We’re not seeing a park that is just for data centres that wants to serve our region. We think we can actually compete globally. There’s growing appetite for more data centres globally. We think West Africa, particularly Nigeria and Togo, can provide a home for attractive data centres,” he said. The partnership comes as Nigeria seeks to expand its domestic cloud computing and data hosting capacity amid growing demand for digital services, artificial intelligence and online transactions. In August, the Federal Government unveiled its National Digital Cloud Policy, targeting 750m within 24 months to develop the country’s cloud and data infrastructure ecosystem. The policy is intended to encourage domestic and international providers to invest in data centres, cloud infrastructure and AI computing capacity, while positioning Nigeria as a regional hub for digital services.
